SCI_HEAVIER_FASTER.label: Thinks heavier objects fall faster
SCI_HEAVIER_FASTER.explanation: Believes mass makes things fall faster, even when air resistance is not involved.

SCI_MASS_WEIGHT.label: Confuses mass with weight
SCI_MASS_WEIGHT.explanation: Thinks mass changes on the Moon, or that weight is measured in kilograms.

SCI_MOTION_NEEDS_FORCE.label: Thinks a moving object needs a constant force to keep moving
SCI_MOTION_NEEDS_FORCE.explanation: Believes the 'force of the push' gets used up, instead of friction slowing the object.

SCI_REST_NO_FORCE.label: Thinks objects at rest have no forces on them
SCI_REST_NO_FORCE.explanation: Misses balanced forces, like the table pushing up on a book.

gravity_and_weight.title: Gravity, mass and weight
gravity_and_weight.big_idea: Mass is how much matter something has and never changes from place to place. Weight is the pull of gravity, measured in newtons. Without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall at the same rate.
steps: Mass (kg) = amount of matter. Weight (N) = force of gravity on that matter.
On the Moon gravity is about 1/6 as strong, so weight drops to about 1/6. Mass stays the same.
Gravity pulls harder on a heavier object, but it is also harder to speed up, so both fall at the same rate.
In real life, air resistance can slow light or spread-out objects, like a feather or a flat sheet of paper.
gravity_and_weight.sense_check: Astronauts on the Moon dropped a hammer and a feather: they landed together, because there is no air there.

worked_examples.prompt: A heavy and a light ball are dropped together with no air resistance. Which lands first?
worked_examples.answer: They land at the same time
steps: No air resistance.
All objects fall with the same acceleration.
They land together.

worked_examples.prompt: An object's mass is 6 kg on Earth. What is its mass on the Moon?
steps: Mass is the amount of matter.

forces_and_motion.title: Forces and motion
forces_and_motion.big_idea: An object does not need a force to KEEP moving; it needs a force to start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn. Things slow down on Earth because of friction and air resistance. Still objects usually have forces on them that are balanced.
steps: Ask: is the motion changing? Only unbalanced forces change motion.
Moving at a steady speed in a straight line means the forces are balanced.
Something slowing down has a force against its motion, usually friction or air resistance.
Something sitting still has balanced forces, like gravity down and a push up from the table.
forces_and_motion.sense_check: A puck on ice glides much further than on carpet. Same push, less friction: the push isn't 'used up'.

worked_examples.prompt: A ball rolls across a carpet and stops. What stopped it?
steps: The ball was moving, then slowed down.
Slowing down needs a force against the motion.
That force is friction from the carpet.

worked_examples.prompt: A book rests on a table. What forces act on it?
worked_examples.answer: Gravity down, the table pushing up
steps: Gravity always pulls the book down.
The book isn't falling, so something pushes up.
The table's push balances gravity.
